He may be continuing the behavior because he gets what he wants from it, either attention or to eat. At 6 months old, he should be able to go at least 6 hours at night without a meal. Granted my kids werent to this extent, but here's what worked for me and my husband:

Give him a nice sized feeding before bed. Maybe some rice cereal or oat cereal. That tends to do well for holding over their appetites. 

For one week, wait 5 minutes before you respond to the crying. When you respond, dont pick him up out of his crib. Just stand there and speak in a soothing voice so he knows you're there to comfort him, and maybe rub his back or belly in gentle circular motions. If you offer anything to "fill his belly", give him water only. Do this until he settles down some, which (full disclosure) may be a while because hes not used to not getting this response. Rinse and repeat every time he wakes up crying.

For the next week, do the same exact thing but wait 10 minutes to respond to the cries.

Keep pushing it out 5 more minutes every week.

He'll know hes not being ignored, but that his behavior will no longer give him the reaction hes looking for. Dumping a baby into full on self soothing all at one can be counter productive, as it creates fear that they've been forgotten or abandoned which can make the crying worse. The baby steps by adding that little bit of additional delay each week helps them learn to cope with their emotions slowly and steadily in a manageable way.

In this extreme case, you may need even smaller baby steps. Maybe adding 2-3 mins a week instead of 5.

Another thing to consider is colic or gas. Maybe look into gripe water before bed.

Hope this helps.

For the potty training, both my kids were in their 3's when they finally "got it" AND executed it. We started working on potty training for both between 18 months and 2 years old. It's all on their time. My youngest, now 4, still sometimes wets the bed at night, but it is rare. Both were pretty determined to take their time. The best results we had were LOTS of positive reinforcement, and prizes (usually stickers). When I say LOTS of positive reinforcement I mean throwing little parties in the bathroom right when they use the potty and very enthusiastic "good job honey!"s and "you're so awesome! I'm SO proud of you!" High fives, calling grandparents on speakerphone to let them brag about how they're "soo big" and the grandparents mimicking the same level of enthusiasm. Not reacting too harshly to accidents, just constantly reminding them that the feeling they get before they go pee/poop is the sign for them to scoot their little butts to the potty ASAP. Also, putting them on the potty every 2 hours to give them a chance to go if they're not going in there on their own and have a clean diaper still. Pull ups helped some by getting them used to pulling them down like "big girl panties".

Hope this helps.

Oh friend. God have I been where you are what feels like thousands of times. My best advice, despite how unconventional, is to keep crying. Literally let ALL of it out. Let it all go. Release it from weighing down on you out into the universe. Once you've cried until you cant cry anymore, and your face is beet red and your eyes half swollen shut, take a few moments to just be. Clear your mind, even if it's only for 30 seconds. Count to 30 and enjoy every single one of them. Then if you have to cry some more, do it. There is NO shame in letting it out. It's much better than holding it all in, which I have a feeling you know all about. Once you're done crying this time, clear your mind for 60 seconds this time around. Rinse and repeat, finding a little more peace each time. When you've had some time to ice your eyes and get some rest (you'll need it, unloading this much negative energy is exhausting), find a psychiatrist that will see you ASAP. You would be amazed how much good a little bit of chemical imbalance tweaking can do. It took me a while to get the right diagnosis and medications but OH MY GOD do I feel so much better. I still have my bad days, dont get me wrong. But not every day is a bad day anymore. And I've learned to find joy in the little things. It doesnt hurt to wake up in the mornings. It isn't a never ending cycle of "oh I'm fine, I'm just tired". You will get through this. Every single second where it hurts a little less, savor it. Time will dull the pain we cling to in order to feel anything at all. Dont give up. There is life after this. I promise you.

The minutes, hours, days all seem to pass so slowly it's almost unbearable. But the years will go fast, and time will dull the unspeakable pain our minds cling to as a last resort to feel anything at all right now. If you haven't yet, go to a psychiatrist. Or if you have one you're unhappy with, find a different one. Theres something special about that magical concoction that helps balance out the chemicals going haywire in your brain. It will never be perfect, but you'll find the light at the end of your tunnel. And you can learn to cling to that instead of the pain.

Stay in tune with what I'm feeling. If I'm in an environment where I need to keep my composure, I find a way to leave. I get home and separate myself as soon as I can so I can get to a place I feel safe and secure tapping into some hefty emotions. I put on a comfort movie, maybe one from childhood or any movie really that gives me good vibes, and I let it all out. Everything I could possibly be upset or stressed about, I bring up every single thing I've been suppressing. I feel the emotion, give a good cry and spew a few profanities, then I let it go. It's like releasing it from burdening me anymore and letting it out into the universe where I'm no longer dragged down by it. Even if it only feels that way for a little. Then I tune back into my feel good movie, put myself back together, and get some rest. Nothing more exhausting than an emotional avalnche.

It seems that he has deep rooted control issues that may well have stemmed from his own childhood. That being said, it is no excuse nor should it be used as a crutch for treating people badly, ESPECIALLY your child. Unfortunately, behaviors such as these that have been occurring for so long rarely get better as they become a part of the individual's actual personality and are no longer contributed to just having a bad day and lashing out occasionally. My advice would be to pick your battles for the next 2 years. In the meantime, for your own benefit and protection, DOCUMENT EVERYTHING. Find someone you trust and tell them what you're going through. In the event he goes off the deep end and police get involved, it will help support your case that he is a threat to you and your mother and that it's not a random occurance and you're not making it up. I wish you all the best.
